title: Extinction of the Neanderthals
summary: Neanderthals, the archaic humans of Europe and western and central Asia, vanished from the archaeological record by about 41,000–39,000 years ago, after a few thousand years of overlap with incoming Homo sapiens; part of their DNA survives in people outside Africa.
card: Radiocarbon dating of 40 sites from Spain to Russia places the end of the Neanderthal-made Mousterian stone industry at 41,030–39,260 calibrated years before present, with populations disappearing region by region rather than all at once. Neanderthals and modern humans shared Europe for roughly 2,600–5,400 years and interbred, so about 1.5–2.1% of the genome of people outside Africa is Neanderthal-derived. Claims of later survival in southern Iberia are still disputed, and the cause is debated between climate stress, small populations, competition and assimilation.
what:
Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis) lived across Europe and southwestern to central Asia from about 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago, according to the Smithsonian's Human Origins Program. They made Mousterian tools struck from prepared stone cores, controlled fire, made clothing and buried some of their dead. Their extinction is dated chiefly by the last Mousterian layers and the last Neanderthal fossils.

The most widely cited chronology is that of Higham and colleagues (2014), who dated about 200 samples of bone, charcoal and shell from 40 sites between Spain and Russia with improved accelerator radiocarbon methods, including ultrafiltration of bone collagen to remove younger contaminating carbon. Their Bayesian model places the end of the Mousterian across Europe at 41,030–39,260 calibrated years before present (cal BP, counted back from 1950 CE) at 95.4% probability. The Châtelperronian, a so-called transitional industry often attributed to Neanderthals, ended at about the same time. The disappearance was staggered: the authors describe a mosaic in which Neanderthal and modern human groups occupied different parts of Europe for 2,600–5,400 years.

The two populations interbred. The draft Neanderthal genome (Green et al. 2010), built from three bones from Vindija Cave in Croatia plus smaller samples from Spain, Germany and Russia, showed that Neanderthals share more genetic variants with non-Africans than with Africans, and the high-coverage genome from Denisova Cave in the Altai (Prüfer et al. 2014) put the Neanderthal-derived share of non-African genomes at about 1.5–2.1%.

The end date is disputed at the margins. Finlayson and colleagues (2006) argued that Neanderthals survived at Gorham's Cave, Gibraltar, until about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, and Zilhão and colleagues (2017) argue that the Mousterian lasted south of the Ebro valley until about 37,000 years ago; Wood and colleagues (2013) and Higham's team found the southern Iberian late dates unreliable. Why Neanderthals disappeared is also unresolved: climate stress, small and inbred populations, competition with modern humans and absorption into their populations all have advocates.

uncertainty.note: Start is the beginning of overlap with Homo sapiens in Europe, c. 45,000 cal BP (early Uluzzian dates reported in the 2014 Oxford/Tübingen release); combining Higham et al.'s 2,600–5,400-year overlap with their end date implies an overlap start of roughly 46,430–41,860 cal BP, which sets the start range. End is the midpoint of the 95.4% range for the end of the Mousterian, 41,030–39,260 cal BP (Higham et al. 2014). Conversions use year = 1950 − cal BP. Disputed later survival is not included in the range: southern Iberian Mousterian to c. 37,100–36,500 years ago (Zilhão et al. 2017, year ≈ −35,150 to −34,550) and Gorham's Cave to c. 28,000 radiocarbon (uncalibrated) years BP (Finlayson et al. 2006).

how: No single mechanism is agreed, but the sequence is fairly clear. (1) Modern humans reached Europe while Neanderthals still lived there: the Uluzzian of Italy, which Higham's team associates with the earliest dated modern humans in Europe, has early dates of about 45,000 years ago. (2) Stalagmites from Ascunsă and Tăușoare caves in the Romanian Carpathians record two severe cold, dry stadials, Greenland Stadial 12 (about 44.3–43.3 ka) and Greenland Stadial 10 (about 40.8–40.2 ka). Near-sterile archaeological layers in the Danube basin and across the Châtelperronian area coincide with them, and Staubwasser and colleagues argue that spreading steppe emptied Neanderthal territories region by region, which modern humans, who seem to have been better adapted to steppe, then reoccupied. (3) Neanderthal numbers were already small: genetic estimates cited by Vaesen and colleagues put their effective population at no more than about 3,000–3,900 over their last 400,000 years, and the Altai Neanderthal's parents were related about as closely as half-siblings. (4) Population models show that groups this small can die out within 10,000 years through reproduction-related Allee effects, inbreeding and chance fluctuations, even without competitors; modern humans may have hastened this by fragmenting Neanderthal ranges. (5) Interbreeding moved Neanderthal DNA into modern human populations, and Villa and Roebroeks argue that low density, gene flow and a shrinking range ended in genetic swamping and assimilation. (6) By 41,030–39,260 cal BP the Mousterian had ended across Europe, with any later survival in southern Iberia still disputed.
why_it_matters: The Neanderthals' disappearance left Homo sapiens as the only human population in Europe, after Neanderthals had lived there and in western and central Asia for some 360,000 years. It was not a clean break. Because the two populations met and interbred, about 1.5–2.1% of the genome of everyone with non-African ancestry today is Neanderthal-derived, and Denisovans in the Altai also carried Neanderthal DNA; that inheritance is a direct, measurable consequence of the contact that preceded the extinction. The event also changed how scholars think about human uniqueness. Villa and Roebroeks found no archaeologically visible inferiority in Neanderthal technology, subsistence or social life, and UNESCO cites Gorham's Cave engravings older than 39,000 years as evidence of Neanderthal abstract thought, so the extinction can no longer be told simply as superior newcomers replacing inferior natives. Dating it drove a methodological shift as well: ultrafiltration showed that many young radiocarbon dates were contaminated, rewriting chronologies of the Middle-to-Upper Palaeolithic transition from Iberia to Russia. Had Neanderthals survived, people outside Africa might today share the planet with a second kind of human instead of carrying fragments of its genome; yet Vaesen's models suggest that, being so few, they might have vanished even if modern humans had never arrived.

related.because: The dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa brought modern humans into Neanderthal territory, creating the overlap, interbreeding and possible competition or range fragmentation that most explanations of the extinction invoke.

perspectives.holder: Higham et al. (2014), Nature; University of Oxford-led team
perspectives.account: With ultrafiltered radiocarbon dates from 40 sites, the Mousterian ends across Europe at 41,030–39,260 cal BP, at different times in different regions, after a 2,600–5,400-year overlap with modern humans. The team could not confirm proposed later refuges in Iberia or at Gorham's Cave and attributes many younger dates to contamination.

perspectives.holder: Finlayson, Giles Pacheco, Rodríguez-Vidal et al. (2006), Nature; Gibraltar Museum
perspectives.account: Hearth charcoal dates from Gorham's Cave show Neanderthals surviving there until about 28,000 radiocarbon years ago, long after modern humans arrived, in isolated southern refuges.

perspectives.holder: Zilhão and Pettitt (2006), Before Farming; Paul Mellars as reported by Nature News
perspectives.account: The Gorham's samples are microscopic, scattered and not ordered by depth; the young dates more likely belong to Upper Palaeolithic use of the cave, and Middle Palaeolithic occupation lasted to about 32,000–30,000 radiocarbon years ago but not later. Mellars warned that small amounts of contamination make dates too young.

perspectives.holder: Zilhão et al. (2017), Heliyon (the Ebro Frontier model)
perspectives.account: In Murcia the Mousterian ends no earlier than about 37,100 years ago and the Aurignacian begins by about 36,500, so Neanderthals persisted south of the Ebro at least 3,000 years after their disappearance elsewhere, behind a biogeographical barrier.

Of 11 southern Iberian sites tested, only Jarama VI and Zafarraya yielded datable bone, and both gave ages at least 10,000 radiocarbon years older than before; late Neanderthal survival in the south rests on at most one possible site, Cueva Antón.

Cold, arid stadials GS12 and GS10 expanded steppe and emptied Neanderthal regions at different times, letting better-adapted modern humans repopulate them; the authors note causality is not fully demonstrated.

perspectives.holder: Vaesen, Scherjon, Hemerik and Verpoorte (2019), PLOS ONE (small-population null model)
perspectives.account: Inbreeding, reproduction-related Allee effects and random demographic swings could have extinguished Neanderthal populations of 50 to 5,000 within 10,000 years without competition or climate change; any role of modern humans was probably indirect.

The archaeological record shows no Neanderthal inferiority in weapons, subsistence or social organisation; disappearance was a protracted process of low density, interbreeding and a shrinking range ending in genetic swamping, though interbreeding may have been too limited for full assimilation.

perspectives.holder: Smithsonian Human Origins Program; competition models summarised by Vaesen et al. (2019)
perspectives.account: Modern humans spreading into Europe during a cold period may have prevented Neanderthals from re-expanding into favoured areas, and many scholars propose that modern humans out-competed them for resources; whether climate or competition mattered more remains open.

importance.justification: The disappearance of the last widespread archaic human population of western Eurasia left Homo sapiens alone in Europe and left Neanderthal DNA in all people of non-African descent, a standard turning point in human-evolution teaching.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the final end date (Higham's 41,030–39,260 cal BP versus disputed southern Iberian persistence to c. 37 ka) and of the start bound, which is approximate; the main pin at Gorham's Cave is a reference site for a range-wide process, and Higham 2014 was read only as its abstract and press release.
parent_reconciliation: Parent species-homo-neanderthalensis is not yet written and has no numbers; its last-appearance date should match this record (end of the Mousterian 41,030–39,260 cal BP, Higham et al. 2014).
